additions.title: SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
additions.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
additions.locator: Principle 4 ('Independent model validation') and Principle 4.1 (the independent validation function); Principle 2.5 (Internal Audit); para 1.5 (in effect 17 May 2024)
additions.quote: Firms should have a validation process that provides ongoing, independent, and effective challenge to model development and use.
additions.why: The clearest UK supervisory expectation of independent review of models, AI models included. Banks should have a validation function giving an objective, unbiased and critical opinion, and internal audit should periodically assess the effectiveness of the whole model risk framework. Applies to banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval; a benchmark elsewhere, not a rule. A supervisory statement of expectations, in effect from 17 May 2024.

additions.title: AI Act, Article 43: Conformity assessment (AI Act Service Desk copy)
additions.locator: Article 43(1) and (2), paragraph 2 marked AMENDED; Commission summary at the head of the page
additions.quote: based on internal control as referred to in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body
additions.why: The Commission's own copy, not the Official Journal; it says the text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version of the AI Act as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes. Shows how limited compulsory third-party review is even under the EU Act: for the high-risk uses in points 2 to 8 of Annex III (employment, credit, education and others) the provider assesses its own conformity by internal control, with no independent notified body; a notified body is involved for biometrics in defined cases and for AI in regulated products. A duty on providers, not deployers; high-risk rules are not yet in application.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
additions.locator: Section 5.3 (Measure), introductory text, document page 28; Table 3, MEASURE 1.3
additions.quote: Processes for independent review can improve the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases
additions.why: International comparator. A voluntary United States framework that builds independence into measurement: MEASURE 1.3 asks that internal experts who were not front-line developers, or independent assessors, take part in regular assessments. Supports the brief's point that the reviewer should be independent of those who built or run the system. Voluntary; no audit or certification scheme attaches to it.

additions.title: Notice of Adoption of Final Rule: Use of Automated Employment Decision Tools (6 RCNY Chapter 5, Subchapter T)
additions.publisher: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
additions.locator: Section 5-300, definition of 'Independent auditor'; section 5-301(a) (bias audit within the past year)
additions.quote: a person or group that is capable of exercising objective and impartial judgment on all issues within the scope of a bias audit
additions.why: International comparator: a rare example of law that compels an independent audit of an AI system. An employer in New York City may not use an automated hiring tool unless it has had a bias audit in the past year by an independent auditor, defined to exclude anyone involved in using, developing or distributing the tool. A city rule covering hiring and promotion tools and bias only; it has no force in the UK and says nothing of governance more widely. The notice prints no adoption date; the year is taken from its hearing dates (January 2023) and the file path (April 2023).

additions.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
additions.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by The National Archives
additions.locator: Paragraph 199 (Ground 5, public sector equality duty); paragraph 201
additions.quote: either directly or by way of independent verification, that the software program in this case does not have an unacceptable bias
additions.why: A UK court treating independent verification as part of what a reasonable deployer does. The police force had never sought to satisfy itself, directly or by independent verification, that its facial recognition software was free of unacceptable race or sex bias, and so had not done all it reasonably could to meet the public sector equality duty. Applies to public authorities under the Equality Act 2010 section 149; it does not create a general duty to commission an audit.

additions.title: Ensuring statistical models command public confidence: learning lessons from the approach to developing models for awarding grades in the UK in 2020
additions.locator: Section 3.4.1.1 ('Engagement with commissioners of the model and others who can help ensure the results meet the need'); section 3.3.1.1 (external challenge through Red Teams or independent advisory panels)
additions.quote: the qualification regulators could have made greater use of opportunities for independent challenge to the overall approach
additions.why: An official review of a public algorithm failure, the 2020 exam grading models in all four UK nations. The statistics regulator found that more independent challenge might have helped secure public confidence, and recommends that anyone developing a model fully explore opportunities for it. About statistical models in the public sector in exceptional circumstances; a regulator's review, not a statutory inquiry.

additions.title: Government Response: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
additions.publisher: Australian Government, Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
additions.locator: Recommendation 17.2 ('Establishment of a body to monitor and audit automated decision-making') and the Government's response, p.22
additions.quote: with the power to monitor and audit automated decision-making processes
additions.why: An official inquiry concluding that automated decision-making needs outside audit. The Royal Commission recommended a body with power to monitor and audit automated decision-making for its technical aspects and for fairness, bias and usability; the Australian Government accepted the recommendation. Read in the Government's response, which reproduces the recommendation: the Royal Commission's own site did not respond today. Australian public sector; acceptance is a commitment to consider, not a body in being.

additions.title: Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance
additions.publisher: Inioluwa Deborah Raji, Peggy Xu, Colleen Honigsberg and Daniel E. Ho (arXiv; AAAI/ACM AIES 2022)
additions.quote: the turn toward audits alone is unlikely to achieve actual algorithmic accountability
additions.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper, read on the authors' arXiv copy. Compares audit regimes in finance, environment and health and concludes that audits alone are unlikely to deliver accountability: what matters is the institutional design around them, including how third parties are able to take part. A review and argument, not new data. Only the abstract is quoted.

additions.title: AI auditing: The Broken Bus on the Road to AI Accountability
additions.publisher: Abeba Birhane, Ryan Steed, Victor Ojewale, Briana Vecchione and Inioluwa Deborah Raji (arXiv; IEEE SaTML 2024)
additions.quote: We find that only a subset of AI audit studies translate to desired accountability outcomes.
additions.why: Evidence for the criterion's top level, findings that change practice. The authors classify AI audits done by regulators, law firms, civil society, journalists, academics and consultancies and assess what each achieved; only some led to any change. Supports asking what a review altered, not whether one took place. Accepted conference paper read on arXiv; a review of published audits, so unpublished internal audits are outside it.

additions.title: Auditing large language models: a three-layered approach
additions.publisher: Jakob Mökander, Jonas Schuett, Hannah Rose Kirk and Luciano Floridi (arXiv; AI and Ethics, 2023)
additions.quote: it is important to remain realistic about what auditing can reasonably be expected to achieve
additions.why: How to scope a review of generative AI. Proposes three linked audits: of the provider's governance, of the model before release, and of each application built on it. Candid about limits, including whether such models can be audited at all. A journal article read on the authors' arXiv copy; a proposed method, not a tested one.

additions.title: The IIA's Three Lines Model: an update of the Three Lines of Defense
additions.locator: Principle 5 ('Third line independence'); Principle 4 ('Third line roles')
additions.quote: Internal audit's independence from the responsibilities of management is critical to its objectivity, authority, and credibility.
additions.why: The model behind the phrase 'third line'. Sets out what makes assurance independent inside an organisation: accountability to the governing body, unfettered access to people and data, and freedom from bias or interference. Helps a board tell self-review (first and second line) from independent review. A professional body's position paper, not a standard and not about AI; copyright 2020, file marked 'Updated September 2024'.

rejected.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (peer review requirement), Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat
rejected.reason: Blocked: HTTP 403 'Request Rejected'. Not bypassed. It would have been the comparator for mandatory peer review.

rejected.title: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, Report (2023)
rejected.reason: The Royal Commission's site did not respond (no HTTP response within 30 seconds, two URLs). A university-hosted copy exists and was not used; the Australian Government's response, which reproduces the recommendation, is cited instead.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC 42006 (requirements for bodies auditing and certifying AI management systems)
rejected.reason: Not re-tried: iso.org returned HTTP 403 on 2 October and again today on another standard page. Paid standard.

rejected.title: CDEI, The roadmap to an effective AI assurance ecosystem (December 2021)
rejected.reason: Reachable, but superseded by the 2024 and 2025 DSIT assurance documents already on the list; adding it would pad.

rejected.title: Raji et al., Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing (arXiv:2001.00973)
rejected.reason: Read (abstract). About internal audit during development by a model developer; less relevant to independent review of a deployer's governance than the three papers kept.

rejected.title: Lam et al., A Framework for Assurance Audits of Algorithmic Systems (arXiv:2401.14908)
rejected.reason: Read (abstract). Overlaps with the papers kept; left out to avoid a fourth research item on the same point.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. 'No general law requires an independent audit of AI governance' holds on what was read: even the EU AI Act leaves most Annex III high-risk systems to the provider's own internal control (Article 43(2)). The brief's own caveat can now be narrowed: for PRA-regulated banks SS1/23 (in effect 17 May 2024) does expect independent model validation and periodic internal audit of the model risk framework, a supervisory expectation the brief does not mention.
